questions.question: Which command checks the installed version of Git?
questions.explanation: `git --version` prints the installed Git version. This is the standard way to verify Git is correctly installed on your system.

questions.question: Which command sets your Git username globally?
questions.explanation: `--global` applies the setting to all repositories on your machine. Without it, the setting only applies to the current repository (`--local`).

questions.question: Where does `git config --global` store settings?

options.B: In a file called .gitconfig in your home directory

questions.explanation: Global config is stored in `~/.gitconfig` (or `C:\Users\YourName\.gitconfig` on Windows). Local config is stored in `.git/config` inside each repository.

questions.question: Which command lists all your current Git configuration settings?
questions.explanation: `git config --list` prints all configuration values from system, global, and local scopes. It is the fastest way to verify your name and email are set correctly.

questions.question: Why should your Git email match your GitHub account email?

options.A: It makes git commit run faster
options.B: GitHub uses the email to link commits to your GitHub profile and show contributions
options.C: Git will refuse to commit if they don't match
options.D: It is required only for private repositories

questions.explanation: GitHub matches the email in your commits to your GitHub account. If they differ, your commits appear as an unknown user and your contribution graph won't show the work.

questions.question: On Windows, which terminal is recommended for running Git commands?

options.B: Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows)
options.D: Git requires a graphical application on Windows

questions.explanation: Git Bash provides a Unix-like terminal on Windows with full Git support. PowerShell and Command Prompt also work but Git Bash is most consistent with tutorials.

questions.question: Which config scope affects only the current repository?
questions.explanation: `--local` scope writes config to `.git/config` inside the current repository only. This overrides global settings for that specific project.

questions.question:
What does the following command do?

git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

options.A: Sets VS Code as the default text editor for Git
options.D: Links Git to your GitHub account

questions.explanation: This sets VS Code as Git's default editor for writing commit messages and resolving merge conflicts. `--wait` tells Git to wait until you close the VS Code window before continuing.

questions.question: If `git --version` returns 'git version 2.43.0', what does this confirm?

options.A: Git is running on GitHub version 2.43
options.B: Git is correctly installed and accessible from the terminal
options.C: You are using an outdated version of Git
options.D: You need to update Git before using it

questions.explanation: Any output from `git --version` confirms Git is installed and your terminal can find it. Version 2.x is current and all features in this programme work on 2.x.

questions.question: Which command sets the default branch name to 'main' for new repositories?
questions.explanation: GitHub now uses 'main' as the default branch. Setting `init.defaultBranch main` globally means every new `git init` will start with a branch called 'main' instead of 'master'.
